en: EUSTACHE : Beatrice! What makes me any more deserving than Dérieux or Varignon, who are starving to death with their wives and kids? I was lucky... unmerited, insulting luck... Why are you shaking your head?
BEATRICE : I only think that if you imagine you see our life more clearly by looking at it through what that woman thinks of it...
EUSTACHE : That woman!... You see...
BEATRICE : You are certainly mistaken. Of course I might be unfair, but she strikes me as being envious.
EUSTACHE : What an error! She doesn't envy me, she pities me...
BEATRICE : The idea!
EUSTACHE : She thinks I've grown bourgeois, degraded... You can laugh.
BEATRICE : I'm not laughing, you're hurt.
EUSTACHE : It's intolerable to me.
BEATRICE, sadly : I can see that.
EUSTACHE : And she is probably right... Besides, even if she were envious, as you say, it would only be the toll of her bad luck.
BEATRICE : Yes, but admit that under those circumstances, her opinion would lose all value.
EUSTACHE : How do you explain, then, that her contempt cuts me so deeply?
BEATRICE : Her contempt! That's too much! What right does that little nobody have to judge you? Say whatever you like; if she was dismissed, I am sure they had good reasons.
EUSTACHE : Beatrice! Do you dismiss a civil servant like a domestic servant?
BEATRICE : Actually, when I think about it... wasn't she a little in love with you, that Gertrude, back in the day?
EUSTACHE : I have no idea! What a way to reason! Always seeing romance everywhere, sentimental complications...
BEATRICE : You know, that's very important in life.
EUSTACHE : Far less than people say. It's bourgeois novelists who have that obsession.
BEATRICE : Eustache!

EUSTACHE : Since they are paid—literally—never to ask the real questions, the only ones that count, the ones that would disrupt their readers' habits, they fill their books with this drivel... Why are you looking at me that way?
BEATRICE, with emotion : You are still so young, such a child!
EUSTACHE : Come off it! (A car horn is heard.) That's your parents.
BEATRICE : Are you coming?
EUSTACHE : There's no need for both of us to rush out. (Beatrice has gone out; Eustache remains on the threshold; raised voices are heard; Eustache frowns.) These family effusions...
[SCENE IV]
THE SAME, DURAND-FRESNEL, MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL, MAXIME.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : Please, Bichette... Hello, Eustache; how—
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : are you?... Tell your brother to be more careful, he drives like a madman; nobody listens to me.
DURAND-FRESNEL, to Eustache : How are you, my friend?
MAXIME, holding out his hand to Eustache : Everything still all right?
EUSTACHE : Thanks.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : On our way here, we just stopped by to ask after poor Madame Obernai...
DURAND-FRESNEL, to Eustache : Have you seen the papers?
EUSTACHE : No.
DURAND-FRESNEL : The Executive Committee's decision?...
EUSTACHE : Well?
DURAND-FRESNEL : Practically speaking, it's a vote of no confidence in the government; resignation is inevitable.
EUSTACHE : What do you say to that?

MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : Bichette, I am absolutely certain I told you; I even telephoned you about it. Follow my example, keep a notebook; a little note is so quickly jotted down... I am quite annoyed that you didn't ask after her. Gustave!
DURAND-FRESNEL : You surely understand there are pros and cons. If I take the viewpoint of party discipline...
EUSTACHE : I must confess I don't give a damn about party discipline.
DURAND-FRESNEL : Oh no, Eustache, really.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : Gustave!
EUSTACHE : To begin with, it isn't my party.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : Beatrice didn't think to ask after Madame Obernai...
DURAND-FRESNEL : If you're already kicking over the traces...
EUSTACHE : What?
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : Gustave, did you hear me?
MAXIME : Look, Mama, there's no use shouting yourself hoarse. They're talking politics.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : Always politics... Listen to me, my child, I'm not one to give advice, but I know that in your place, I would send, oh I don't know... a cyclamen or a little azalea.
BEATRICE, conciliatory : We'll see.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : I've already seemed to notice... your husband and you consider yourselves too easily excused from taking into account
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : certain obligations that have their importance. Gustave!
DURAND-FRESNEL : You ought to understand that with the dangers of reaction taking shape on all sides, if you don't do your part...
EUSTACHE : Who are you talking about?
DURAND-FRESNEL : The Socialists, confound it! Let me tell you plainly: your attitude is intolerable.
EUSTACHE : I don't understand.
DURAND-FRESNEL : If you had thirty years of defending the Republic behind you...
EUSTACHE : I am forced to observe that behind the shield of those grand words, you have allowed the worst abuses to perpetuate themselves.
DURAND-FRESNEL : What abuses?
EUSTACHE : And that your party has never ceased colluding with the powers of money.
DURAND-FRESNEL, bellowing : What abuses?
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : Gustave, please! Don't you agree with me that Beatrice ought to send a cyclamen or an azalea to Madame Obernai? Please think before answering.
EUSTACHE : I am opposed to it, quite simply. Obernai is one of the worst scoundrels of our time...
DURAND-FRESNEL : What?
EUSTACHE : He's on the payroll of the secret funds.
DURAND-FRESNEL : And what of it?... Besides, you forget that among my colleagues in the Senate, he was one of those who supported you most warmly when you received your decoration.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : Eustache! You don't wear it anymore.
EUSTACHE : No.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : But that's absurd. Gustave!
EUSTACHE : You know perfectly well that without Beatrice's insistence I would have refused it.
DURAND-FRESNEL : That's news to me.
EUSTACHE : But I admit that even that would have been attaching too much importance to such a bauble.
DURAND-FRESNEL : My friend, do you realize that an opponent of the Republic wouldn't speak any differently?
EUSTACHE : Which republic?
MAXIME : I can see where you're heading with your soviets... enough, enough... as for me, those Moscow people have disgusted me ever since they became militarists.
DURAND-FRESNEL : You don't take the German peril into account.

MAXIME : Leave us alone with the German peril! All we have to do is give them back their colonies, and if they need a piece of Ukraine or Lithuania, whatever, well then, let them go to it... I certainly won't stand in their way... Peace, peace!
DURAND-FRESNEL : My boy, you speak of these things with such flippancy... I was reading last night in Le Temps... There are principles on which one cannot compromise.
MAXIME : Oh come off it, principles—don't make me laugh...

DURAND-FRESNEL, to Eustache : I sometimes wonder if there isn't a void in their education... These young people seem so cynical to me... At their age, I remember... I know very well that we won our spurs in the shadow of the Dreyfus Affair... Eh? But you, my friend, being of an intermediate generation and after all closer to my son's, you are an idealist as well...
EUSTACHE : Excuse me. Thoroughgoing materialist.
DURAND-FRESNEL : Yes... if you like... agreed; but all in all it amounts to the same thing.
EUSTACHE : We don't speak the same language. When I denounce the abuses of present-day society, you don't even understand what it's about.
DURAND-FRESNEL : Allow me, allow me. I have always been in the vanguard of those demanding education and well-being for the people...
EUSTACHE : There is no question of reforms. Present-day society cannot be reformed. You are a closet conservative, nothing more.
DURAND-FRESNEL, to Beatrice : I cannot fathom how you can let your husband insult me.
BEATRICE : But I don't know, you see, Papa; Eustache might be right.
DURAND-FRESNEL : You have alienated my child's heart from me.
BEATRICE : No, Papa, you are very sweet.
DURAND-FRESNEL : That is not the issue.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL, to Maxime : Maxime, go get the cake (she pronounces it 'keck') from the car.
BEATRICE : I'm going to make the tea.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL, appalled : You don't have a maid?
BEATRICE : It's Sunday. Raymonde has gone out.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : I always specify that my housemaid shall not go out on reception Sundays. I give

MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : an afternoon off during the week to make up for it. I made inquiries. All my friends do the same. Otherwise you lose all authority. Your little maid already strikes me as not being properly trained.
EUSTACHE : Trained! That's it. Trained!...
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : Will you please hold your tongue, my dear man; men understand nothing of these matters.
EUSTACHE : The regime of privilege. A pre-1789 mentality!
[SCENE V]
THE SAME, GISELA.
GISELA, entering while rubbing her eyes, like someone barely awake : Ah! I slept so well.
BEATRICE : Let me introduce you to my parents. (To Madame Durand-Fresnel.) Mama, I told you about our friend Madame Schnee.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : But certainly. (Ceremoniously.) Good day, Madame. (The two men bow.)
GISELA : I was so sleepy. I think it is something in the air.
BEATRICE : People always say the climate of Paris makes one sleepy.
GISELA : Besides, I love to sleep. Already back in Germany...
BEATRICE : I'm going to make the tea.
GISELA, pleading : You permit that I come help you? (Lower, but still too loud.) I am intimidated.
BEATRICE : As you wish, Gisela. See you shortly. (She goes out with Gisela.)
[SCENE VI]
DURAND-FRESNEL, lowering his voice : Tell me, Eustache, have you made inquiries?
EUSTACHE : What do you mean?
DURAND-FRESNEL : I remind you that one must be careful. God knows I am happy to see my country persevere in its traditions of hospitality...
MAXIME : Spare us the development.

DURAND-FRESNEL : But I learn on good authority (Maxime laughs.)... Well, what?... that under cover of this wave of emigration washing over our shores, many—let us speak plainly—undesirables have found a way to slip in here.
EUSTACHE, very dryly : I have known Schnee for ten years...
DURAND-FRESNEL : You must surely be aware that unfortunately some of those whose republican convictions seemed most firmly established have succumbed to the illusions of dictatorship...
MAXIME : What's the matter with you, Papa? You're not sick? Your language is so flowery... and the blood is rushing to your head.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : Maxime, you are insufferable...
DURAND-FRESNEL : It would be painful to all of us to think that you were harboring a disguised Hitlerite under your roof.
EUSTACHE, barely controlling himself : Werner is no more a Hitlerite than I am.
DURAND-FRESNEL : Good, good, I ask for nothing better than to believe you.
MAXIME : When will they make up their minds to close our borders to all this riffraff? You'll see, all these Jews will end up infiltrating everywhere.
EUSTACHE : Werner is not Jewish.
MAXIME : Then what the hell is he doing here, for God's sake!
EUSTACHE : He left of his own free will.
MAXIME : We don't have to cater to these whims.
EUSTACHE : Do you even know what you're talking about? Not everyone is in the mood to lick Hitler's boots.
MAXIME : Between Hitler's boots and Stalin's, what's the difference? No, but I'm asking you! (Eustache has walked out, slamming the door.) Your son-in-law is going completely round the bend.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : These arguments are splitting my head open.
MAXIME : Papa isn't saying anything; he's afraid of compromising himself.

DURAND-FRESNEL, after a pause : I admire you both; you pass judgment, you lay down the law... without the slightest basis for evaluation. The plight of these political refugees is infinitely deserving of pity. On the other hand, we must take into account the interests of our own unemployed. If France is obliged to a certain degree (sneer from Maxime) to remain the land of asylum welcoming all defenders of freedom without distinction, she cannot be asked to neglect her legitimate interests either...
MAXIME : So? So? The conclusion?
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : Maxime, you are interrupting your father. What strange manners.
DURAND-FRESNEL, with satisfaction : The elements of the problem are singularly complex.
EUSTACHE, storming back in like a whirlwind, brandishing a photograph : Take a look at this!
MAXIME : What is this corpse?
EUSTACHE : That is Rudolf Schönthal upon his arrival from Germany.
MAXIME : And so what?
EUSTACHE : They beat him savagely, they trampled him.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : I don't want to hear these horrors, they affect me too much.

MAXIME : As if your friends in the Cheka didn't have just as many to their credit! When did you ever hold meetings to protest Bolshevik atrocities? You have a double standard, you people... Oh! And as for me, I'm fed up. Let all those people devour each other. It's none of our business.
EUSTACHE : An attitude like yours justifies those who want to enslave us. When a country has sunk to such a degree of spinelessness and baseness, it is ripe for slavery.

DURAND-FRESNEL : That is going too far, my friend; I am far from endorsing Maxime's oversimplified judgments; between Moscow and Berlin, believe me, I know how to make the distinction. Nonetheless, it remains true...
MAXIME, yelling in his face : What? What? What? (Durand-Fresnel throws himself back, covering his face with both hands.)
[SCENE VII]
THE SAME, BEATRICE, GISELA.
(They wheel in a small tea trolley carrying a teapot, a sugar bowl, etc., and cakes.)
BEATRICE : There, if you don't mind, we'll put the trolley here in front of the window. (During the following scene, Gisela will help her serve the tea.)
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : Maxime, I told you to go get the cake. Thank you, Bichette, you know I no longer take tea. Doctor Pausanias has forbidden it.
EUSTACHE : What did you say?
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : He's my Greek; I'm delighted with him. In ten days I've lost fifteen hundred grams. You really should tell Papa to try his treatment.
DURAND-FRESNEL : With my workload, I cannot indulge in a weight-loss cure. I shall go to Brides next summer if necessary.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL, to Beatrice, in an undertone : Don't you think your father is getting a bit paunchy, Bichette? Don't you? It pains me so...
DURAND-FRESNEL, sourly : What?
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : Eustache, on the other hand, is scrawny. Are you sure he is assimilating his food properly?
BEATRICE : I don't know, Mama.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : You ought to take him to Pausanias. He's remarkable. And now he charges a flat fee.
MAXIME : How much does that work out to per kilo?
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : What are you saying?
MAXIME, as Gisela pours him some tea : Thanks, thanks, no water. The tea is always dishwater at my sister's.

DURAND-FRESNEL, to Eustache : Have you seen that new periodical... what is it called again? I have good friends on the editorial staff. But what a surprise to find that Champmartin's signature on the front page.
MAXIME : Montmartin.
DURAND-FRESNEL : It hardly matters. He's a militant Catholic... Is that his place, I ask you? My dear friend, there's no hiding it: the priests are regaining their strength.
GISELA, softly, to Beatrice : What does it mean, that expression?

DURAND-FRESNEL : And that is something an old Radical like me, a devoted advocate of the secular ideal, cannot witness without astonishment, and I would say without consternation. Sometimes at night I wake up, and I call to mind the great elders, those I call the pioneers: Henri Brisson, Émile Combes... What would they say if they were among us? What advice would they give us? They died too soon.
MAXIME : But I say, your Brisson would be a centenarian by now, or what?...
DURAND-FRESNEL : Human life is too short.
GISELA, softly, to Beatrice : I do not agree.

DURAND-FRESNEL : A man cannot, how shall I put it? see his work through to the very end; it slips from his grasp, and sometimes crumbles to pieces. It is one of the most disheartening thoughts I know... How do you explain, Eustache, this relative success of clerical maneuvering? For my part, I don't conceal it from you, it is yet another consequence of that terrible war.
EUSTACHE : It doesn't interest me. It's probably linked to the crisis. It's like pilgrimages in times of famine in backward countries.

DURAND-FRESNEL : But we are not a backward country, confound it! If I may venture to use that somewhat worn comparison, yet after all still true, it is France—and she almost alone today with England, though I mistrust those Puritans—who still holds the torch of civilization in her hand... There is something in all this that I cannot explain.
MAXIME, mimicking him : Something de-mon-i-a-cal...
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : Maxime! Enough of that!
MAXIME : Come on, Mama, don't yap every time...
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : I yap? Bichette... I don't know; there is something in the atmosphere of this house that attacks one's nerves.
BEATRICE : What do you mean, Mama?
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : I don't know, my child, I simply note the fact: whenever I leave your house, I don't feel myself.
GISELA, opening her eyes wide : You are unwell?
[SCENE VIII]
THE SAME, WERNER.
(Werner has entered silently; he is pale, his features drawn; he hasn't taken the time to remove his overcoat.)
GISELA, catching sight of him : Werner!
BEATRICE : What! Is that you, Werner? We didn't hear you come in...
EUSTACHE : And so?
WERNER : If you would be so kind as to introduce me...

BEATRICE : Our friend Monsieur Schnee; my parents; my brother Maxime. (Werner bows somewhat stiffly; it is clear his thoughts are elsewhere.) The journey wasn't too trying? (Werner answers only with a convulsive shrug of his shoulders.)

GISELA : Ach! Come now, Werner, you're not going to keep your overcoat on... it's not all that handsome to begin with. (Werner takes it off and puts it over the back of a chair.) But go hang it in the hallway, really. (Werner goes out.) I don't know what's the matter with him.
BEATRICE : He looks tormented. I'm afraid his poor friend...
GISELA : That Rudolf, he gets on my nerves... (Werner comes back in. A silence.)
BEATRICE : Will you have a cup of tea, Werner?
WERNER : It isn't necessary. (She serves him.)
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : You come from Switzerland, Monsieur?
WERNER : I beg your pardon?
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : It is a beautiful country; we have stayed there several times, leaving us with very fond memories.
DURAND-FRESNEL : Our French Alps are enough for me: what tourist riches in this country! When will we learn to exploit them? (The sentence falls flat.)
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL : It is true that Chamonix, the Dauphiné, Pralognan-la-Vanoise...
WERNER, to Beatrice : Thank you, that's enough.
GISELA : When did you arrive?
WERNER : I was already here this morning.
GISELA : What were you doing all this time?
WERNER : I had lunch with Rudolf's mother.
GISELA : That wasn't necessary.
WERNER : I think it was.
GISELA : That Frau Schönthal, she is also tedious.
EUSTACHE : Has she settled in Paris?

WERNER : She lives in a room on the Rue d'Enghien, near the Place de la République, over that way. You can't see properly. You have to turn on the light even in the daytime... A tiny little room. There's only space for the bed, a chair, a small table with a washbasin. And in the courtyard there is, how do you say? eine Schmied.
EUSTACHE : A forge.
WERNER : Or something like that. All day long, you hear... bang... bang... bang...
BEATRICE : I suppose she isn't in her room very often?
WERNER : She never goes out, she's almost an invalid...
EUSTACHE, in an undertone : It's horrible.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL, rising as if propelled by a spring : It is getting late... We shall have to make our way back to our eighth.
WERNER, astonished : You live on the eighth floor?
MAXIME : No, no, don't worry. But my mother always thinks in terms of arrondissements.

DURAND-FRESNEL, to Eustache : No hard feelings, my friend. We traded a few barbs... But after all, that's the price we pay for a singularly precious good, and one which neither of us is any more willing to give up than the other.

MAXIME, pompously : And that good, ladies and gentlemen, is called freedom! (He puffs out his cheeks and hums some revolutionary anthem through closed lips. This comic effect falls completely flat. Werner puts his hand to his head with an overwhelmed air.)
BEATRICE, to Werner : You look exhausted.
WERNER : It doesn't matter. (Madame Durand-Fresnel has gone out; Beatrice follows her.)

DURAND-FRESNEL, to Eustache : If there's any news on the ministerial front, I'll telephone you. Bourbillon may resurface, you understand. In guarded terms, of course... I'll say: 'The Y is running on normal schedule again'; that's the bus that serves the Ministry of National Education, you understand.
MAXIME : What a conspirator... the soul of a Carbonaro.
MADAME DURAND-FRESNEL, from outside, in a shrill voice : Gustave! Maxime! (They go out.)
[SCENE IX]
GISELA, to Werner, with irritation : What is it, for goodness' sake?
WERNER : Ah! Leave me alone...
EUSTACHE, with a touch of irritation : You won't tell us anything, Werner... Is he worse?
WERNER, softly : Very bad. Probably by the end of the week...
EUSTACHE : Did you want to stay by his side?
WERNER : His mother had to go there. She will leave tonight.
GISELA : You gave her money?
WERNER : Obviously.
GISELA : And what will she do with it? Will she even go? Ist doch ganz unvernünftig. We already have so little.
WERNER : That's enough.
GISELA : It won't be enough.
WERNER : Schluss damit. (Beatrice has returned.)
BEATRICE : I can sense you are worrying terribly.
WERNER : More than worrying...
EUSTACHE : Perhaps you are exaggerating.
GISELA : Naturally. Rudolf, he has, how do you say, an incredible endurance...

WERNER : You haven't seen him... He's a ghost... He didn't smile, even when I arrived... Not once... And he used to smile all the time... In his face you see nothing but his eyes... so large, immense... He looked at me as if he were reproaching me for something.
GISELA : Das find'ich aber fein... You sacrificed everything for him...
WERNER, to Beatrice : I wanted to stay. But he said I had to come back and explain to his mother... Besides, I'm going back to Paris now to put her on the train.
GISELA : Unsinn! She has no need of you.
BEATRICE : You are exhausted, Werner. Couldn't Eustache or I go to the station in your place?
WERNER : It is perhaps the last thing I can do for him... (In an undertone.) Rudolf, he was a man.
EUSTACHE : What?
WERNER, seeming to look past Eustache : I am only saying: Rudolf was a man. Höheres gibt es überhaupt nicht.
BEATRICE : Werner, you are unhappy. But I assure you that you have friends in us who will never abandon you. Eustache has told me often, he loves you like a brother, doesn't he?
EUSTACHE, after a second : Yes, yes... besides, he knows it well. (Werner looks at him. Eustache lowers his eyes; the curtain falls.)
